focus.text: An adjective clause, also called a relative clause, is a group of words that describes a noun. It begins with who, which, that, whose, where or when, and it sits straight after the noun it describes. Relative clauses let you join two short sentences into one, so your writing carries more information without repeating names. The pronoun you choose depends on what the noun is and on the job it does inside the clause, and the commas you use change the meaning.

summaryTable.caption: Relative pronouns at a glance
rows: The mentor **who** trains us is from Huế.
The app **which** tracks my revision is free.
people or things, in defining clauses only
The essay **that** I submitted was too short.
A student **whose** notes are clear revises faster.
The café **where** we study opens at seven.

pretest.sentence: The volunteer who collected the plastic bottles is in my class.
pretest.reason: *who* introduces a clause about a person, and here it is the subject of *collected*.

pretest.sentence: My neighbour which teaches maths lives on the fourth floor.
pretest.reason: *who* for people, *which* for things: *My neighbour who teaches maths*.

pretest.sentence: This is the photo that I took it in Đà Nẵng last summer.
pretest.reason: *that* has already replaced the object, so *it* must go.

pretest.sentence: The bus that stops outside our school is always full.
pretest.reason: *that* can introduce a defining clause about a thing.

pretest.sentence: I have a friend whose her father runs a bakery in Cần Thơ.
The film that we watched on Friday was based on a true story.
pretest.reason: *that* is the object of *watched*, which is a normal object relative clause.

pretest.sentence: Cần Thơ, which sits on the Hậu River, is famous for its floating market.
pretest.reason: The city is already identified, so extra information goes between commas with *which*.

pretest.sentence: The laptop, that I bought online, arrived three days late.
pretest.reason: *that* cannot follow a comma; a non-defining clause takes *which*.

pretest.sentence: The woman to whom I sent the form replied within an hour.
pretest.reason: After a preposition, use *whom* for a person, not *who* or *that*.

pretest.sentence: The students attended the workshop were given certificates.
pretest.reason: A reduced clause needs *attending*, or write the full clause *who attended*.

context.title: The Saturday library
context.paragraph: Every Saturday morning a group of students who live near the old market in Huế meets at a small library. The library, which opened three years ago, is run by volunteers. Most of them are teachers whose classes finish early at the weekend. The children that come to the sessions choose their own books, and the room where they read is bright and quiet. Last month the group started a reading log which records how many pages each child finishes. Minh, who manages the log, says the numbers surprised everybody. The prize that the library gives every term is not money but a new book, and the day when the prizes are handed out is the busiest of all.
targets: who live near the old market in Huế
whose classes finish early at the weekend
which records how many pages each child finishes
that the library gives every term
when the prizes are handed out

sections.title: Forming adjective clauses with who, which and that

table.caption: Relative pronouns for people and things
columns: The noun and its job in the clause
rows: a person, subject of the clause
The coach **who trains** our team is from Đà Nẵng.
a person, object of the clause
The coach **(who) I met** yesterday is from Đà Nẵng.
a thing, subject of the clause
The app **which blocks** notifications is free.
a thing, object of the clause
The app **(which) I use** most is free.

notes: In a defining clause you may leave the pronoun out when it is the **object**: *the film (that) we watched*. You can never leave it out when it is the **subject**: *the film that won the prize*.

items.stem: The engineer ___ designed the new bridge studied in Hà Nội.
I still use the dictionary ___ my aunt gave me in grade 9.
items.reason: The noun is a thing (*the dictionary*), so *that* or *which* is correct.

items.stem: The students ___ finish the survey early can leave.
items.reason: *who* is already the subject of *finish*, so no extra pronoun is needed.

items.stem: The message ___ yesterday has still not arrived.
items.reason: *that* replaces the object of *sent*, so *it* must go.

items.stem: Lan has a cousin ___ works for an airline in Đà Nẵng.
items.reason: The pronoun is the subject of *works*, so use *who*; *whom* is only for objects.

sections.title: Using subject and object relative clauses

rules.text: Put the adjective clause straight after the noun it describes, so the reader knows what it refers to.

examples.text: The scholarship **that covers tuition** is open to second-year students.
I finally found the notes **which my brother lent me** last term.

rules.text: Use *who* for people and *which* for things. *That* works for both, but only in a defining clause.

examples.text: The nurse **who** looked after my grandmother works nights.
The bus **which** goes to the airport leaves every twenty minutes.

rules.text: The relative pronoun already stands for the noun, so never repeat it with *it*, *him* or *them* inside the clause.

examples.text: The article **that I read** last night changed my view on plastic.
Huy is the friend **who** I trust most.

rules.text: When the pronoun is the object, you may drop it in informal writing, but keep it in essays so the sentence stays easy to follow.

examples.text: The survey **(that) we carried out** covered ninety households.

notes: A common slip is to leave an extra pronoun behind: *the phone that I bought it*. The relative pronoun has already replaced the object, so *it* has no job left.
tips: Relative clauses are a quick way to vary your sentences. Instead of two short ones, join them: *Đà Lạt attracts tourists. It has a cool climate.* becomes *Đà Lạt, **which has a cool climate**, attracts tourists.*

sections.title: Forming clauses with whose, where and when

table.caption: Clauses that begin with whose, where and when
rows: a classmate **whose notes** are always complete
the market **where** my mother buys fish
the year **when** the old factory closed

notes: *whose* is followed straight by a noun, with no article: *a teacher whose advice changed my plans*. *where* and *when* are followed by a full clause: *the school where she teaches*.

sentences: Our school has a small garden.
The biology club looks after it.
model: Our school has a small garden which the biology club looks after.
Our school has a small garden that the biology club looks after.
items.reason: *it* becomes the relative pronoun at the front of the clause, so nothing follows *looks after*.

sentences: I want to thank the librarian.
She found the article for me.
model: I want to thank the librarian who found the article for me.
I want to thank the librarian that found the article for me.
items.reason: *she* is the subject of the second sentence, so it becomes *who*.

model: Khoa lent me a bicycle whose front light was broken.
Khoa lent me a bicycle which had a broken front light.
items.reason: *whose* replaces *its* and is followed straight by the noun *front light*.

model: We finally reached the village where my grandparents grew up.
We finally reached the village in which my grandparents grew up.
items.reason: *where* replaces *there*, so no preposition is left at the end.

sentences: I will never forget the afternoon.
The exam results came out then.
model: I will never forget the afternoon when the exam results came out.
I will never forget the afternoon on which the exam results came out.
items.reason: *when* replaces the time expression, so *then* disappears.

sections.title: Using defining and non-defining clauses

rules.text: A defining clause says which one you mean. It takes no commas, and it can begin with *that*.

examples.text: The students **who submitted their essays late** lost five marks.
The report **that the committee published** runs to sixty pages.

rules.text: A non-defining clause adds extra information about a noun the reader can already identify. Put it between commas and use *which* or *who*, never *that*.

examples.text: Cần Thơ, **which lies in the Mekong Delta**, hosts a floating market.
bold: which lies in the Mekong Delta

examples.text: My supervisor, **who studied in Australia**, marks very quickly.

rules.text: The commas change the meaning, so check them before you submit. Without commas you limit the group; with commas you describe all of it.

examples.text: The teachers **who speak French** attended the meeting. (only some of them)
The teachers, **who speak French**, attended the meeting. (all of them)

notes: A non-defining clause can also comment on the whole sentence before it: *The bus arrived late, which meant we missed the first talk.* Use *which* here, never *what*.
tips: In IELTS Writing Task 2, a non-defining clause lets you add a definition without starting a new sentence: *Remote work, which was rare before 2020, is now normal in many offices.*

items.sentence: The scientist which discovered the fungus works in Đà Lạt.
This is the recipe that my aunt taught it to me last summer.
items.reason: *that* already stands for the recipe, so *it* must go.

items.sentence: Huế, that is famous for its royal tombs, attracts visitors all year.
items.reason: A non-defining clause after a comma takes *which*, not *that*.

items.sentence: The candidates who they passed the first round will be interviewed.
items.reason: *who* is already the subject of *passed*, so the extra pronoun is wrong.

items.sentence: The teacher whose her students won the prize was interviewed on television.
items.reason: *whose* already means *her*, so the possessive is written twice.

sections.title: Reducing an adjective clause

table.caption: Full clause to reduced clause
rows: the form **which was signed** last week
the bridge **that connects** the two districts
the only person **who can help** you

notes: You can only reduce a clause when the relative pronoun is the **subject**. *The book that I read* cannot become *the book read*, because *that* is the object there.
The infinitive reduction works after *the only*, *the first*, *the last* and superlatives: *the first student to finish*.

sections.title: Using prepositions with which and whom

rules.text: In formal writing, move the preposition in front of *which* or *whom*. In everyday writing it can stay at the end of the clause.

examples.text: The colleague **with whom** I share an office speaks four languages.
The theory **on which** the article is based dates from 1970.

rules.text: After a preposition, use *whom* for people and *which* for things. *Who* and *that* are not possible there.

examples.text: The students **for whom** the course was designed are complete beginners.
This is the fund **from which** the scholarships are paid.

rules.text: Use a quantifier with *of which* or *of whom* to add a figure about the group you have just named.

examples.text: The survey reached 300 residents, **most of whom** supported the plan.
The school offers ten clubs, **three of which** meet at the weekend.

tips: *Whom* is only needed after a preposition or in very formal writing. If the preposition stays at the end, *who* is perfectly acceptable: *the manager who I spoke to*.

editing.text: Last year my sister joined a small theatre group which it meets every Sunday in a community hall near our house. The group, that was started by three former students, now has about thirty members. Most of them are young people who they work during the week, so rehearsals always begin after lunch. The director is a woman whose her patience surprises everybody. The play which they performed in April told the story of a fishing village on the coast. My uncle he built most of the set from old wood and painted it himself. The number of students who buy tickets have doubled since the first show, and the hall which they rehearse is now far too small. Everyone which I spoke to after the performance said the same thing: this group deserves a bigger stage.

errors.reason: *which* is already the subject of the clause, so *it* is repeated.
After a comma a non-defining clause takes *which*, never *that*.
*who* is already the subject of *work*, so the extra pronoun must go.
*whose* already means *her*, so the possessive is written twice.
The noun is already the subject, so the pronoun is not repeated after it.
The head noun is *the number*, not *students*, so the verb is singular.
A place takes *where*, or *which* with a preposition (*in which*).

topics.prompt: Write an email to a friend in Cần Thơ describing a club at your school. Mention the person who runs it, the room where it meets, and one activity that you enjoy most.
checklist: At least four sentences contain an adjective clause.
*who* is used for people and *which* or *that* for things.
No clause repeats the noun with an extra *it*, *him* or *them*.

topics.prompt: Some people think every student should do voluntary work before leaving school. Give your opinion, describing the kinds of students who benefit most and the projects that suit them.
checklist: At least two defining clauses identify which group you mean, with no commas.
At least one non-defining clause, between commas, adds extra information.
*that* never appears straight after a comma.

topics.prompt: Describe a place in your city that most visitors miss. Explain where it is, who goes there and why it matters to the people who live nearby.
checklist: At least one clause begins with *where* and one with *whose*.
At least one clause is reduced, for example *the market selling fruit* or *the bridge built in 1998*.
Every clause sits straight after the noun it describes.
